HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Befunge-93 (Chris Pressey, 1993) runs on a 2D grid: > < ^ v steer the instruction pointer, _ and | are conditional turns, and @ ends the program. It can rewrite its own grid as it runs.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (truncated) — an ordered list like this, plus a starting number, is a complete program in this language. The rest of the list has been cut.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: There is almost nothing here except numbers and one repeated separator.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Fractran (John Conway) is Turing complete with nothing but a list of fractions: multiply the current number by the first fraction that gives an integer, and repeat. Its most famous list generates prime numbers.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — backticks and single letters. There are no variables, no numbers and no keywords hiding anywhere else in the language.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.weakHint: Two kinds of marks do almost everything here.
HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Unlambda (David Madore) is functional programming stripped to combinators — `k, `s and `i — plus .x, which prints the character x. It was designed to make functional programming feel as awkward as Brainfuck makes imperative programming feel.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — only six distinct characters appear in this entire language, and this fragment uses all of them.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Hexagony (Martin Ender) runs on a hexagonal grid — the source code itself forms a hexagon of characters, and the instruction pointer moves in six directions, wrapping around the edges.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.note: // Tiny excerpt (1–2 lines) — the tail of a one-line program and the row beneath it. The pointer wraps around the tank’s edges and works off a stack.

HARD_FRAGMENTS.fact: Rockstar (Dylan Beattie, 2018) makes programs read as song lyrics: “Say” prints, poetic literals spell numbers out in words, and “Midnight takes your heart and your soul” defines a function of two arguments.
